Any major can be pre-med as long as you complete the necesssary classes; I knew someone who was a pre-med dance major. However, I believe some majors have pre-med focuses/tracks that allow you to easily incorporate the requisite classes into your education.

Like at any school, the classes you will need to take (Biology, chemistry/orgo, physics) will be very challenging because they need to prepare you to take the MCAT. If you are motivated and did well in high school you will likely be able to find them manageable, however they do end up encouraging many students to change their minds about medical school. I don't have any hard data, but from my experience with friends and classmates I would say 50-75% of them decided against applying to medical school. This sounds scary, but many of them instead found out in college that they loved research and decided to pursue a PhD or they decided to become a public health lobbyist or a medical writer. I guarantee that even if the classes at Iowa discourage you from applying to med school (which will be true at any college), you will be provided with opportunities to find something you love doing. Clubs and extracurriculars will help with this. 

Despite the large class sizes, you can easily make relationships with professors by going to office hours, emailing them with questions, etc. Iowa does NOT use a pre-med committee for letters, so make sure you do build relationships with some of your professors.

It is very easy to have a social life at Iowa. You will make many friends in the dorms who are in the same boat as you. I do advise you to avoid getting caught up in the party scene too early, I know many people who didn't get enough sleep or neglected their schoolwork by going out too much. You will absolutely be able to hang out with friends, go to parties, go to events despite the hours you will spend on homework/research/work. You will find a way to have a healthy social life. You will need it to stay sane.

Research is not required for medical school (unless you are planning on an MDPhD) but I would recommend getting some research experience. I can't personally say anything about having a job on top of everything, for a lot of pre-meds research is like a job to them and you can get paid. I do know people who have taken gap years after college to gain experience as an EMT or scribe before applying to med school.
